collins.hedgehog: None. Collins's comparison company swung back and forth between consumer products and health care: consumer products in 1979, health care in 1980, back to diversification and consumer in 1981, toward Merck-style pharma in 1987, and back to consumer brands in the early 1990s. It never committed to one concept.
hedgehog_key_points: lurched between consumer-products and pharmaceutical identities
each new CEO reset the strategy
collins.stop_doing: Stop lurching between consumer and pharmaceutical strategies, and stop the restructure-with-each-CEO cycle. Stop buying unrelated businesses (bakery, optical, later medical devices) as a substitute for a clear concept.
stop_doing_key_points: stop resetting strategy with each new CEO
collins.leader_type: Not Level 5. Collins counts three major restructurings between 1979 and 1998, roughly one per CEO. Each new leader launched his own program and halted his predecessor's momentum, a textbook doom loop.
brutal_facts: profit margins down about 40% and ROE about 9% in 1979
regulatory and legal problems across several lines
a distant No. 2 to Gillette in shaving

later_history: Entenmann's was sold to General Foods in 1982 for $315M. IMED was bought for $468M in 1982 and sold in 1986 for $163.5M. Five units were divested in 1982-86 and the workforce was cut from about 61,000 to 32,000; ROE recovered to 32% by 1986. Another reorganization followed in 1991 under Melvin Goodes. Later it co-marketed Lipitor. Pfizer acquired the company in 2000 after a hostile bid, ending its independence, and auctioned off Schick (to Energizer, 2003).
notes: Direct comparison company for A09. The year-by-year lurching (1979-1990s) comes from Collins's own 'Good to Great' article on jimcollins.com, paraphrased. Sources conflict on 1979-80 titles (Hagan as chairman, Williams as CEO or president), so the dossier says only that a new chairman and chief executive took over in Year -1.
